name: ConceptGraph authored computing course v1
provenance: Original educational fixture written for this repository. Saved answers are editorial examples. Graphs for the benchmark must be extracted by the configured LLM; no expected graph is injected.

pages.title: HTTP
pages.text: HTTP defines requests and responses between a client and a server. A request contains a method, target, headers, and sometimes a body. A response contains a status code, headers, and optionally a body. HTTP itself does not encrypt the message. In this course, HTTP is a prerequisite for understanding TLS in web communication, and TLS is a prerequisite for understanding HTTPS. Learn this sequence: HTTP, then TLS, then HTTPS.

pages.title: TLS
pages.text: TLS protects data in transit using encryption and integrity checks. A certificate helps the client authenticate the server during the handshake. A browser checks that the certificate matches the requested hostname and chains to a trusted authority. TLS does not decide whether a signed-in user can read a particular document. HTTP is a prerequisite for studying TLS in this web course; TLS is a prerequisite for HTTPS.

pages.title: HTTPS
pages.text: HTTPS carries HTTP messages over TLS. To understand HTTPS, study TLS first and HTTP before TLS. This makes HTTP a foundational prerequisite two steps before HTTPS. HTTPS protects traffic between browser and server against passive reading and modification in transit. It does not repair application authorization bugs, prevent a malicious server from storing data, or guarantee that a website is honest.

pages.title: DNS
pages.text: DNS resolves domain names to records such as IP addresses. A resolver can reuse a cached answer until its time to live expires. A DNS lookup does not prove that an application is healthy. After locating a server, the browser still needs a successful connection and an HTTP response. DNS caching and HTTP caching operate at different layers: one reuses name resolution results, the other reuses application responses.

pages.title: HTTP Caching
pages.text: HTTP caching reuses a stored response when its freshness rules permit. Cache-Control can specify private responses or prohibit storage with no-store. An ETag is a validator that can support conditional requests and avoid downloading an unchanged representation. Never assume a shared cache may safely store a personalized response. This response cache differs from a database index, which accelerates locating rows without storing an HTTP response.

pages.title: Status Codes
pages.text: An HTTP 401 response means authentication is required or the supplied credentials are not accepted. An HTTP 403 response means the request is forbidden; it can occur even when identity is known. HTTP 429 indicates too many requests and can include a Retry-After header. HTTP 503 indicates that a service is temporarily unavailable. Clients should distinguish these cases rather than report every failure as an invalid password.

pages.title: Authentication
pages.text: Authentication establishes the identity of a caller using credentials or an existing session. Authorization decides whether that identity may perform a specific action on a resource. In this course authentication is a prerequisite for authorization, and authorization is a prerequisite for document access control. A successful login alone does not grant permission to every PDF in an application.

pages.title: Authorization
pages.text: Authorization evaluates whether a caller may perform an action on a resource. For a private PDF, compare the verified caller identity with the document owner or an explicit sharing rule. Authentication is a prerequisite for authorization. Authorization is a prerequisite for document access control. These checks belong on the server and must cover previews, retrieval, downloads, deletion, and graph queries, even if the interface hides buttons.

pages.title: Document Access Control
pages.text: Document access control enforces ownership or sharing rules on every operation involving a document. Its direct prerequisite is authorization; authentication is the foundational prerequisite before authorization. Protect vector searches and graph traversals with the same document scope used for PDF previews. Guessing an upload identifier must never grant access. HTTPS protects transport, but it cannot replace these resource permission checks.

pages.title: Signed Sessions
pages.text: A signed session cookie lets a server detect tampering and verify an expiry time. HttpOnly prevents page JavaScript from reading the cookie; Secure restricts transmission to HTTPS. A signature provides integrity, not secrecy, so session contents must not include secrets that require encryption. A stateless signed cookie does not by itself create per-user document ownership or provide instant revocation without additional state.

pages.title: Phishing
pages.text: Phishing uses deceptive messages or websites to persuade a person to disclose credentials or perform an unsafe action. A message may manufacture urgency to discourage checking the sender. Verify unexpected requests through a separate trusted channel. HTTPS can encrypt a phishing website's traffic, so a secure connection is not proof that the operator is trustworthy. This lesson distinguishes transport protection from human deception.

pages.title: Rate Limits
pages.text: Rate limits bound the number of requests a caller may make in a time window. Expensive AI operations can have a smaller budget than read-only metadata requests. HTTP 429 can tell a client to slow down. Rate limits control consumption but do not establish identity or document ownership. A shared reviewer code often maps all reviewers to one shared request budget and shared workspace.

pages.title: Transactions
pages.text: A database transaction groups related changes into a unit that commits or rolls back. For a document workflow, authoritative metadata can record which processing stage completed. A SQL transaction does not automatically roll back writes made to an external vector database or object store. In this course transactions are a prerequisite for idempotency, and idempotency is a prerequisite for safe retries.

pages.title: Idempotency
pages.text: Idempotency means repeating an operation has the same intended effect as performing it once. Deterministic chunk identifiers and upserts can prevent a repeated ingestion attempt from creating duplicate vectors. Transactions are a prerequisite for studying idempotency in this workflow, and idempotency is a prerequisite for safe retries. Idempotency does not mean every attempt succeeds; the operation must still report failures.

pages.title: Safe Retries
pages.text: Safe retries repeat a transiently failed operation under a bounded attempt budget. Their direct prerequisite is idempotency, whose prerequisite is transactions. Use a delay or backoff when a provider is busy and stop retrying permanent input errors. If an earlier write may already have succeeded, deterministic identifiers help make the next attempt safe. Blindly repeating a non-idempotent action can duplicate data or effects.

pages.title: Compensating Cleanup
pages.text: Compensating cleanup removes partial derived artifacts after a workflow fails across services. A PostgreSQL rollback cannot erase points already written to Qdrant. Delete by the exact upload identifier and preserve authoritative metadata until cleanup can be retried. Cleanup is not a distributed atomic transaction: it can also fail, so record the failure and keep operations idempotent.

pages.title: Vector Search
pages.text: Vector search compares numeric embeddings to locate passages with similar meaning. Filter by the allowed upload identifiers before returning results. A similarity score does not prove that a passage supports the answer. Reranking can compare the question and each candidate more carefully; an evidence threshold can reject weak matches. Vector search complements a concept graph, which stores explicit typed relationships such as prerequisites.

pages.title: Readiness
pages.text: Readiness decides whether a service can accept useful traffic. Required dependencies such as the authoritative database must work. An optional concept graph may be reported as degraded while vector-based answers continue. A healthy process does not prove that an external AI provider has quota. Readiness and rate-limit failures require different operator responses.

saved_examples.question: What should I learn before HTTPS?
saved_examples.answer: Start with HTTP, then TLS, then HTTPS. TLS is the direct prerequisite; HTTP is the foundational prerequisite two steps away. HTTPS protects HTTP traffic in transit, but it does not replace document authorization.

saved_examples.question: Does logging in make every PDF private?
saved_examples.answer: A login verifies identity. The server must separately authorize each document operation using ownership or sharing rules. Apply the same scope to PDF previews, vector retrieval, and graph queries; hiding a button is insufficient.

saved_examples.question: Why can retrying an upload create duplicates?
saved_examples.answer: An earlier write may have succeeded before the caller saw a failure. Retrying safely requires idempotency, such as deterministic chunk IDs and upserts. Bound the retry count and stop on permanent input errors.
